reels2real · Issue #1

The Ad Muter

Watch it work A real ad, covered and muted. 40 seconds on YouTube.

A Mi TV Stick, a laptop, an AI, and a war on Prime Video ads.

Chapter 1 · Movie Nightthe projector, Prime Video, and ads

Movie night at home: the projector on its tripod, Prime Video on the wall. Then the ads started, and there was no skip button. Every break meant grabbing the remote, muting, and remembering to unmute. Pritam wanted the TV to do that by itself and asked Claude to help. Together they started on a test bench: the Mi TV Stick on a small monitor.

Movie night. Projector on, Prime Video on the wall. Then the ads came.
Pritam, every single ad break:
Subscribed… and still seeing ads? Hmmm.
Fine. I'll just mute the ads.CLICK!
Yay! …wait, it's manual. Every. Single. Break.
Let's automate it! Claude, you in?DING!
So Pritam and Claude built a test bench. Mi TV Stick on a small monitor, a webcam on a tripod, and the laptop.
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #12
Chapter 2 · Plan A: The Webcama webcam on a tripod, watching the TV

The first idea was simple: let a camera watch the screen. Pritam set up a USB webcam on a tripod, pointed at the screen, and Claude wrote a small program on the laptop to read its picture. The bright screen blew the first frames out completely. With the exposure turned right down, the app tiles became readable, but everything still depended on the room light and on where the tripod stood.

Plan A: a webcam watches the TV for ads. GLARE!
Exposure down to −7. Now it could read the screen.
Sort of.
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #13
Chapter 3 · Claude Takes the Remoteswitching on developer mode

Claude asked Pritam to switch on Developer options and USB debugging on the stick. From then on it could talk to the stick over Wi-Fi using ADB, Android's debugging connection, and it went through the options one by one, testing each on the real TV. Chromecast could mute the stick but had no idea what was on screen. The Google TV remote link knew which app was open, but not whether an ad was playing. Asking Prime for its on-screen text returned nothing at all.

Device Preferences › About
Buildtap × 7
Developer options › USB debuggingON
You are now a developer!
Tap Build 7 times, then switch on USB debugging.
What did that switch unlock? ADB.
ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is a door Android leaves for app developers. Once USB debugging is on, a computer on the same Wi-Fi can drive the stick: no cable, no extra hardware. That's how Claude, running on the laptop, could see and press things on the TV.
Then Claude took over. Approach after approach:
  • ✗Webcamworks, but glare and room light decide
  • ✗Chromecast mutemutes fine, can't see ads
  • ✗Google TV remote linkknows the app, not the ad
  • ✗Read Prime's text over ADBPrime exposes no text at all
  • ✓ADB screenshotsee the next panel
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #14
Chapter 4 · The Breakthroughan ADB screenshot during a real ad

Then Claude took a screenshot over ADB while an ad was playing. The controls Prime draws on top of the video were perfectly sharp, including the yellow “Ad 0:19” badge in the corner. Counting yellow pixels in that corner was enough: 212 during the ad, none during the movie. No camera, no AI.

Prime protects its video, so the picture came out completely black. But the ad's text overlays were completely visible.
The movie came out black. The badge didn't.
"Ad 0:19"! 212 yellow pixels in the ad, 0 in the movie.
BINGO!
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #15
Chapter 5 · Version 1the first one that worked

The first working version ran on Pritam's laptop. Every couple of seconds it checked whether Prime was open, looked at the badge corner, muted when the yellow “Ad” showed up, and unmuted when it was gone. It only ever undid its own mutes. Then a real ad break arrived in the middle of a movie.

The first idea, the way it was really planned:
Pritam & Claude

Found it. The yellow "Ad" badge: 212 yellow pixels during the ad, 0 in the movie.

Plan: every ~2 s, if Prime is open, screenshot that corner. Badge there → mute. Gone twice in a row → unmute.

Only undo your own mutes. If I muted it myself, leave it alone.

Deal. And if you unmute during an ad, I stay out of it until that break is over.

Make it fun, but above all reliable. Use all the tricks.

Then I'll also read the countdown, and the ad-break dots on the progress bar, to look faster when a break is near.

Small job: one script on your laptop. Starting now.

Version 1, on the laptop:
Is Prime Video open?↓ Screenshot the badge corner↓ Yellow "Ad"? → MUTE↓ Badge gone → UNMUTE (only our own mute) First real break: muted 1 second after the badge appeared. Countdown 110 s. Unmuted 1 second after the ad ended.
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #16
Chapter 6 · Making It Fastthe same night

Version 1 worked, but it was slow. One look at the screen took about 5 seconds on the little stick, so Claude grabbed only the thin strip with the badge instead of the whole picture. Android's normal key command could take up to 10 seconds, so it wrote straight to the stick's virtual remote. It also learned to read the countdown, and Prime's progress bar told it when the next break was due.

Then: make it quick.
One look at the screen:5 s→1.5 s→0.9 s
Only the badge's strip of the screen, not the full picture
One key press:1–10 s→0.5 s
sent straight to the stick's virtual remote
ZOOM!
The gaps in Prime's progress bar are the ad breaks.
One look at the bar, and Claude knew when to check every second instead of every few.
Muted. But something was still bugging Pritam.
Pritam & Claude

The audio is muted, but I can still see the ads.

lightbulb moment

Let's hide the video as well.

Doable. A tiny app on the stick can lay a full-screen cover over Prime whenever the watcher says "ad". The remote keeps working, and the countdown corner stays uncovered.

And if the watcher ever goes quiet, the cover removes itself after a few seconds. The screen can't get stuck dark.

Keep it non-invasive. Go.

THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #17
Chapter 7 · The Coverlater that night

Muting fixed the sound, but the ad was still on screen. That night Claude wrote a small app for the stick that lays a dark frosted cover over the TV while an ad plays. It leaves the badge corner clear so the countdown stays visible, and it removes itself if the watcher goes quiet, so the screen can never get stuck dark.

Later that night, the ad lost its picture too. A frosted cover with its own countdown. Prime's badge corner stays clear. SHHH!
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #18
Chapter 8 · The Pi Takes Overfrom the laptop to the Pi

Version 1 lived on Pritam's laptop, and laptops go to sleep. If it slept in the middle of an ad, the TV could stay muted all evening. So the watcher moved to the Raspberry Pi that already sits on the home network. Claude installed ADB and a text reader for the countdown on the Pi, set the watcher up as a service that starts at boot and restarts itself, and switched the laptop's copy off so the two would never fight over the mute button.

The laptop sleeps. The Pi doesn't.
→ ⇢
The safety note

muted-by-watcher.flag

Before muting, the watcher writes this note. If it crashes mid-ad, the new copy finds the note and unmutes. The TV never stays stuck on mute.

House rules for the Pi
bootstarts by itself
crashrestarts by itself
1watcher per TV, never two: they'd fight over the mute toggle
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #19
Chapter 9 · The Projectora second screen

Next screen: the BenQ GV30 projector, which has its own Android TV dongle inside, the QS01. Same Prime, same yellow badge, but at 720p, so Claude scaled every measurement. Then a surprise: the projector's mute key didn't mute Android at all. It went down a wire to the projector's own speaker chip as a blind on/off toggle. Claude gave the cover app its own mute switch, so the watcher could always tell whether the sound was off.

The second TV
Same badge, smaller screen (720p):
“Go ad free”? I'm already paying for Prime!

Remote: MUTE→QS01→ wire →projector's speaker chipblind toggle: can't tell if it's on or off
Watcher→Cover app→Android mutereadable: the watcher always knows

THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #110
Chapter 10 · Does It Even Need the Pi?one simple question

With two screens working, Pritam asked a simple question: does this really need a Raspberry Pi taking a screenshot every second? Claude looked at what Prime tells Android about playback, the same report that powers the remote's play button. During an ad, Prime still says “playing”, but it takes away seeking. That one change was the whole detector. No screenshots during playback, and faster than the badge watcher.

The question that changed everything:
Pritam & Claude

Does it even need the Pi?

Maybe not. Every video app tells Android what it's doing: playing, paused, which buttons work. Let me watch what Prime says during an ad.

Found it. During an ad, Prime still says playing, but seek, fast-forward and rewind disappear. The number goes 1049455 → 1049095: exactly 360 apart.

So the TV can watch itself?

Yes. One small app on the TV, listening to Prime. No Pi, no screenshots while you watch.

The one ad it can't hear: pause ads. Pause for 5 seconds and Prime shows a still ad, but its status just says “paused”. So the app takes a screenshot only while paused. Covered 5.3 s after the pause.
No Pi, no screenshots. Just the TV looking after itself: A real ad, covered and muted by the app alone. Prime's own “Ad 0:12” still shows in the corner.
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #111
Chapter 11 · Can We Do the Same to YouTube?the next app with ads

Prime was handled. But on the Mi TV Box, YouTube was still playing ads, so Pritam asked the obvious question. Good news: unlike Prime on that box, YouTube's TV app reports its ads honestly. During an ad it says “playing” and takes away seeking, the very same sign. So muting was instant. Even better, many YouTube ads can be skipped after five seconds, so Claude taught the app to spot the Skip button and press OK, the remote's own button, all by itself.

Prime was quiet now. YouTube wasn't.
The question, the evening after:
Pritam & Claude

Can we do the same to YouTube?

YouTube tells Android the same story: during an ad it's playing, but seeking is gone (51 instead of 379).

So: mute and cover the moment an ad starts. And when the Skip button shows up, I'll press OK for you.

Do it.

The real Skip button
I thought the circle was a countdown to Skip. It's the time left in the whole ad. Oops.
The cover leaves this corner open, so the button stays visible.
Meanwhile, at dinner…
I'm going to eat. Songs are playing. Keep watching and refining.
While Pritam ate: no sound blip between two ads in a row (wait 0.8 s before unmuting), and a Skip check every second instead of every two.

THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #112
Chapter 12 · A Nicer Waitmaking the cover fun

The ads were silent and hidden now, but a two-minute break staring at a dark screen that says “AD PLAYING” is still two minutes of nothing. So Pritam turned the cover into something worth looking at: a big clock and date, and a quote that changes every seven seconds, taking turns between English and Hindi. Forty of them, written for this. The corner with Prime's countdown stays open, so you always know how long is left.

Pritam's wish list, one message at a time:
Pritam & Claude

Make the “AD PLAYING” text larger, and add some funny quotes while the ad runs. Make it less boring.

Done: bigger title, and 25 quotes that change every 7 seconds.

Add some quotes in Hindi too.

Show the date and time.

Alternate between Hindi and English.

Done. Clock and date top-left, quotes take turns: English, Hindi, English…

“AD PLAYING” that big isn't important. Put it below the clock.

Moved. Small and quiet under the clock, the quote gets the middle.

THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #113
Chapter 13 · The Demo That Failedfilming the proof

Pritam set up a phone to film a demo on the Mi Stick: a two-minute Prime ad break, covered and muted. It went perfectly, until one ad handed over to the next. The cover vanished for about eleven seconds, and a little sound slipped through. Pritam's guess: the muter had mistaken the end of one ad for the end of the whole break. Claude went through the video frame by frame and through Android's own logs, and found something else. The stick has only 1 GB of memory. Starting the next ad needed a bit more, and Android made room by closing the cover app, twice.

From Pritam's video: the countdown keeps running while the cover is gone.
The sound in the video: two short blips, nothing more.
What really happened, as Android wrote it down:
  1. 0 sNext ad starts. Memory runs out. Android closes the cover app
  2. +1 sAndroid restarts it. It unmutes before checking: the first blip
  3. +5 sStill no memory. Closed again
  4. +9 sRestarted again: the second blip
  5. +12 sCover back up until the break ends
Two guesses, one log:
Pritam & Claude

The cover dropped right after an ad changed. It's not counting the time. It should read the counter.

And the sound did come back.

You're right about the sound: two short blips, one at each restart. But the cover went away 0.24 s after Android closed the app, not because the muter decided anything.

Two fixes. After a restart, the mute and cover go straight back. And I'll teach it to read the countdown, so an ad change can never end the break early.

Do both. Keep Chromecast.

Learning to read the badge: real samples, every digit from 0 to 9. Read 40 out of 40 badges correctly. Now, if the break still has time left, the cover stays put, whatever else happens.
THE AD MUTER · ISSUE #114
Chapter 14 · Lights, Camera, 4×editing the demo video

Pritam filmed a fresh demo for the cover of this comic. It worked perfectly, which was the problem: an ad break is long, and ninety seconds of a calm dark screen makes a slow video. So Claude became the editor. It found exactly where the ad began and ended, sped just that part up four times, cleaned up the sound the phone had picked up from across the room, and trimmed the whole thing to forty seconds. Then it wrote the YouTube title and description too.

The editing brief, straight from Pritam:
Pritam & Claude

The ad runs from 12.8 s to 103.1 s: 90 seconds. At 4× that becomes about 23.

Don't lose the audio. Can we clean it up a bit?

It was recorded from across the room, very quiet. Cutting rumble and hiss, then bringing it up to YouTube level.

End the video at 40 s.

Give relevant text for each field.

Title, description with chapters, tags, category. And set it to Public or Unlisted, or the comic can't show it.
